problem: VLM/LLM long-horizon robot planners depend on scene-specific prompts or prior environment knowledge. Under vague, scene-agnostic instructions (e.g. 'heat the vegetables') they ignore logical and spatial constraints, such as needing to open the microwave before placing food while holding it. They also produce a single fixed plan that breaks when anything changes. Existing LLM multi-robot planners handle only short-horizon tasks and cannot refine their plans.
motivation: Household tasks are long, multi-stage and benefit from several robots working in parallel. Failures often come from constraints the VLM overlooks in a long context, not from low-level control. The paper observes that explicitly checking pre- and post-conditions at each subtask surfaces these missed constraints as reflections. Those reflections can then be reused to evolve better and more parallelizable plans across iterations, without task-specific prompting or fine-tuning.
key_idea: Wrap zero-shot LLM task decomposition in a loop: a VLM checks pre-conditions (to catch planning errors) and post-conditions (to catch execution errors) for every subtask; the reflections are stored in a memory and used to regenerate better initial plans over iterations; the refined plan is then split so a second robot handles the pre-conditions in parallel.
insight: Most failures on reasoning-heavy kitchen tasks come from ignored preconditions, and turning them into explicit checks raises success rates. In Table 1, adding condition checking (CC) lifts TSR from 0–10% to 20–50%, but makes plans long and redundant: IPL rises to 8.5–14 and time grows. Feeding the accumulated reflections back into planning (RE) removes these redundant steps (IPL cut roughly 35–62%) and raises TSR further, for example DefrostInBowl from 20% to 50%. Delegating pre-condition subtasks to a second robot (REMAC) cuts plan length and time further, at a small robustness cost from failure propagation. Reasoning LLMs matter: reflection success averages 12.5% for GPT-4o, 37.5% for DeepSeek-R1 and 82.5% for Grok3.
method: Scene-grounded initial planning: a reasoning LLM (DeepSeek-R1) receives the list of items in scene E and a scene-agnostic instruction I, decomposes I into K subtasks executable by pre-trained language-conditioned low-level policies, and analyzes temporal dependencies between them.

Pre-condition check: before each subtask, a VLM (GPT-4o) looks at the current scene image and the subtask description to judge feasibility. If the subtask is infeasible, the VLM explains why, replans the remaining subtask sequence, and writes the reason into a reflection buffer.

Post-condition check: after each subtask, the VLM judges from the post-execution image whether the subtask succeeded. On failure the subtask is retried and pre-conditions are rechecked; these failures are attributed to the policy and are not stored as reflections.

Iterative self-evolvement: the reflections plus the last iteration's plan are stored in a long-term memory and fed with the scene items and I back to the reasoning LLM. Over multiple iterations this yields a feasible, non-redundant initial plan.

Multi-agent collaboration: once the single robot can do the task reliably, the main agent extracts a main-object-centric plan and summarizes the recorded pre-condition sequence. A second robot is prompted to complete those pre-conditions (e.g. open the microwave, place the pan) in parallel before the main robot needs them.

Benchmark: a two-robot RoboCasa environment with physical controllers and 4 reasoning-difficult tasks (OpenCabinetPnP, OpenMicrowavePnP, DefrostInBowl, HeatOnStove). Each task has 6–8 layouts and 5–12 styles, drawing on 50+ objects, with randomized initialization.

numbers_note: This is a manipulation/mobile-manipulation paper on a self-built RoboCasa benchmark. None of the canonical navigation benchmarks are used, and there are no official splits: 'test' denotes the paper's evaluation runs of 10 random initializations per task. The comparison with baselines (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3 planners, CAPE, REFLECT, REFLECT+CC) is reported only in a figure (Fig. 'Comparison with baselines', 20 experiments per task), with no numeric values in the text. Table 2 also reports per-task reflect success rates for gpt-4o, QwQ, DeepSeek-R1, o3, Qwen3 and Grok3 (averages 12.5/26.25/37.5/62.5/66.25/82.5%). Only two of these are listed above. Headline claims in the text: +40% average success rate and +52.7% efficiency over the single-robot BASE; about 20% lower average subtask duration going from RE to REMAC; at most 5.8% absolute success-rate drop from multi-robot coordination.
results: On four reasoning-difficult RoboCasa kitchen tasks, REMAC raises task success from 0–10% (single-robot BASE) to 30–60%, for example HeatOnStove 60% vs 10% and OpenMicrowavePnP 50% vs 10%. It also has the lowest plan length (IPL 4–7) and time, and the paper reports +40% average success and +52.7% efficiency over BASE. A figure shows RE/REMAC outperforming REFLECT+CC and CAPE. On a real dual-arm mobile robot doing OpenMicrowavePnP, REMAC reaches 25% full-task success in 57.2s, versus 10% in 128.5s for CC and 0% for BASE. Among reasoning models used for reflection, Grok3 is best (82.5% average) and GPT-4o worst (12.5%).
limitations: Very small, self-built evaluation: 4 tasks with 10 trials each (20 in the real world). Baseline comparisons appear only in a figure, and absolute success stays modest (≤60% in simulation, 25% on the real robot).
Relies on repeated iterations on the task to accumulate reflections (test-time trial and error) and on a provided list of scene items. Low-level skills are pre-trained, task-specific policies.

Multi-robot execution suffers from failure propagation: success sometimes drops relative to single-robot RE, e.g. DefrostInBowl 40% vs 50%. Collaboration is limited to two homogeneous robots, with the helper handling pre-conditions.
